Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT (and its alias ML.GENERATE_TEXT)

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING (also available as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING) and AI.EMBED are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  1. Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  2. Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  3. Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin), or Service Usage Admin (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a QuotaExceeded error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support max_error_ratio (such as AI.IF) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as AI.GENERATE) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their status field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The AI.COUNT_TOKENS function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Count the input text tokens for each product review\r\nSELECT\r\n SUM(\r\n AI.COUNT_TOKENS(\r\n CONCAT('Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral: ', review_text),\r\n\r\n endpoint => 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite').result) AS total_input_tokens\r\nFROM\r\n `my_project.my_dataset.product_reviews`;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe080d38a10>)])]>

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Cost: 0.125 × I + 0.75 × O = 100 (I, O in millions of tokens)\r\nRatio: I = 100 × O'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe073b90c10>)])]>

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts max_output_tokens, set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  1. Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  2. Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  3. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

title: Taking the PULSE of Medical Reasoning: Step-Level Retrieval Timing for Knowledge-Grounded Inference
summary: Reliable medical reasoning requires LLMs to dynamically access external biomedical evidence to improve factual trustworthiness and reasoning accuracy. However, indiscriminate retrieval can introduce noise and latency, raising a critical retrieval-timing problem: at each reasoning step, the system must decide whether the model's internal knowledge is reliable or external evidence is needed. We propose PUlSE, a lightweight probing method that uses the model's internal representations as intrinsic signals for step-level retrieval control. Our posterior trajectory analysis reveals that erroneous steps exhibit substantially higher inter-layer volatility than correct ones, suggesting unstable internal knowledge. Based on this finding, PUlSE trains a compact probe on inter-layer geometric features to detect factual errors upon step completion, and uses it as an adaptive trigger for retrieval and step regeneration. Across four medical benchmarks, PUlSE-timed retrieval matches exhaustive per-step retrieval in accuracy while reducing retrieval calls by 72%, and can transfer to an unseen legal domain, indicating potential domain-agnostic generality. Overall, our study provides an initial step toward shifting retrieval-trigger design from surface-level confidence estimates to internal activation dynamics for adaptive access.

title: Predicting Unseen Scientific Interactions: Conditional Flow Models Hallucinate Non-Additive Effects
summary: Conditional generative models are increasingly used for scientific prediction beyond the direct training support. Yet scientific questions often concern whether one intervention changes the effect of another. Such interactions can be of primary interest while explaining little of the total variation, allowing models to appear accurate overall without recovering the relevant scientific effect. It remains unclear how these models learn interactions and when these successfully extrapolate to unseen conditions. We therefore study interaction recovery in flow-matching models using a physiological time-series simulator, drug dose-response data, combinatorial cell perturbations, and molecular conformer generations, where we separate recovery from hallucinated interaction structure. In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held-out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.

title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon
summary: Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, tool use, and environment feedback over extended interactions. Learning from sparse outcome rewards requires weighting trajectories of different lengths and updating the policy while rollouts are still being collected. We examine a single-rollout asynchronous recipe combining Muon, token-averaged loss, truncated importance sampling, and auxiliary length and tool-error penalties. Single-rollout sampling allows asynchronous learning without waiting for multiple trajectories for the same issue. We study optimizer choices and recipe components for repository-level issue resolution across two model families. The evaluated training runs show higher training success with the full recipe than with the baselines.

title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
summary: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.

title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
summary: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.

title: A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
summary: Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.

title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities
summary:
Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output. Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. They can therefore observe how uncertain the model is, but not what it is uncertain about. Consequently, they cannot distinguish between a model that is torn between "big" and "small" and one that is torn between "big" and "huge" when the two pairs receive the same probability distribution.
  We introduce GURI (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity), a lightweight gray-box hallucination detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers. This exposes which alternatives the model considered while preserving the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks, GURI increases mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09% over a probability-only baseline. On the closed-source GPT-4.1 model, mean ROC-AUC increases from 67.39% to 71.84%. Among the three open-weight models, GURI outperforms transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning. For the three open-weight models, cross-dataset transfer between HotpotQA and TriviaQA with the model held fixed improves mean ROC-AUC over transferred LOS-Net by 3.76 points.

title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
summary: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

title: When Protection Overrides Consequences: Understanding Protection Mode in Large Language Model Decision-Making
summary: Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. At lowest effort, at least one of four responses prioritizes the subject on 34.74% of Sol prompts and over 83% of MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-27B prompts; none of four independent human raters does so. Controls show that choices usually track physical risk. We elicit both risks before requesting an action. Some models assess risk incorrectly; others state the correct ordering but still choose the subject. Qwen3.5-27B with thinking shows 100% correct risk ordering but 57.81% subject choice among eligible conversations on eight selected scenes. Attention audits find no stable reduction in attention to relevant facts; removing the stated risk direction reduces object-first choice in dots3-note-prev but not detectably in Qwen3.5-27B. Adding a general "people or animals before property" rule increases subject choice by 19-38 percentage points, whereas factual reminders favor the object by 0.7-5.2 points. Removing naturally generated versions of that rule lowers subject choice by 10-15 points. We also examine whether post-training introduces this pattern. Base models already show Protection Mode; post-training changes justifications more than choices.

title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
summary: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.

title: LAGO: Language Agents with Reusable Growing Options
summary: Long-horizon tasks expose a weakness of monolithic tool-use loops: one agent must decompose, execute, and verify a task within a single trajectory. We introduce LAGO, which treats specialized language agents as reusable temporally extended options. A meta-agent retrieves options from a persistent library or spawns new ones, dispatches sub-tasks, verifies results, and admits successful novel options. The library grows across tasks without updating model weights. On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in both roles resolves 58.6% under single-attempt evaluation with the official Docker evaluator. On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively. Cross-model experiments provide evidence consistent with a role for decomposition quality. A 50-task component ablation finds four fewer resolved tasks without decomposition, two fewer with shuffled reused content, and six fewer without the library. These results support reusable agent-options as a practical abstraction for task streams, while leaving component-level causality task- and model-dependent.

title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
summary: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.

title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
summary: Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student's behavior with the teacher's. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. At each such state, ActionOPD samples actions from both the student and a black-box teacher, rewarding student actions according to their semantic agreement with the sampled teacher actions. Through policy optimization, ActionOPD aligns the student's action-level behavior with the teacher's decisions without requiring reproduction of teacher-written reasoning or access to teacher token probabilities. Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with two teachers on diverse, curated tool-use tasks yields average gains of 3.3-6.9 percentage points across four out-of-distribution benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability, without requiring the teacher and student to share a model family or tokenizer. On $τ^2$-bench, ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. We further explore Self-ActionOPD with a same-model teacher and privileged context. These results establish ActionOPD as a promising approach to agent distillation.

title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
summary: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
summary: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

title: Articulation Upper Bounds for Language Models
summary: Language captures only a subset of the perceptions, intuitions and intents that form meaning between speakers. What, then, are the limits of language? We take steps towards measuring this in LLMs as follows: for a set of concepts, we measure how well each concept can be transmitted between two LLMs as their capabilities scale. This requires novel measurement tools: (1) optimal messages: we introduce a prompt optimization algorithm that beats existing algorithms by up to 14% on benchmarks and accurately estimates prompt upper bounds. (2) A transmission measure: the sender is asked to label text; the receiver then tries to recover the sender's prompt, and recovery is measured; we find this correlates strongly with human label error. With these measures, we use observational scaling laws to study how transmissibility of a concept, conveyed with optimal messages, increases as transmitter and receiver capacity grows: does it asymptote below or above a threshold? Measuring 1.2k concepts in eight domains, we find concepts that (a) can be fully articulated; these concepts usually depend on local patterns, e.g. "joke ends with surprise"; (b) might be articulated by future, stronger models; these rely on whole-text structural patterns, e.g. "story's worldbuilding coherence"; (c) concepts that face articulability limits; these concepts' meaning, we find, is tied to identity and social-group awareness, e.g. "comic voice". Interesting, these same concepts are not all challenging for humans: humans have moderate-to-high levels of agreement in 76% of concepts that LLMs struggle with; articulation limits, we find, are executor relative. Finally, we characterize the nature of improvement in each case: while recoverable concepts can be articulated through definitions and explanations, irrecoverable concepts cannot be transmitted, even with examples, and might require novel learning mechanisms.

title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
summary: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. To address this gap, this paper introduces \textbf{RuleTrek}, a multi-domain benchmark for agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Its rule-grounded construction pipeline extracts structured rule graphs, generates and incrementally composes rule-specific sub-scenarios while ensuring consistency and solvability. To systematically evaluate agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios, RuleTrek assesses three capabilities in interactive workspaces: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs show that the highest RI and RD scores are only 62.47\% and 60.43\%, respectively, while E2E scores range from 26.97\% to 55.29\%. These results demonstrate that current LLM agents face substantial challenges in rule reasoning over complex scenarios. We make our code and dataset publicly available at \href{https://github.com/yuan247/RuleTrek}{RuleTrek}.

title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
summary: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
summary: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
summary: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
summary: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
summary: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. A harness around the workflow's directed acyclic graph (DAG) decides which outputs may be used: it enforces mandatory checks, contains failures to the affected branch, recomputes from tracked versions, adds validators, and releases a result only if a risk model estimates its probability of being invalid as low. Language-model agents work inside the harness, choosing corrective actions and reviewing releases, but cannot override it. On 60 held-out paired instances of two workflows with injected faults, we switched components on and off. Each supplied a different property. Containment and recovery raised the number of correct results. Validation supplied safety: fixed rules without validation released 37 invalid results, while validating every candidate released none. Risk estimation supplied efficiency, matching that safety with 31% fewer validators at somewhat lower yield, although better targeting than random validation was not shown. Lineage evidence helped on one workflow. The language model added no measurable benefit: whether invalid results escaped depended on the harness, not the model. This proof of concept points to a practical path: placing agents inside explicit release-control structure can keep released scientific results trustworthy, and it gives more capable agents a measurable baseline to improve on.

title: xLightGCN: Explainable Graph Neural Network Based Recommendation Systems with Most Influential Peers
summary: Recommendation systems, systems that predict a user's preference for items in order to curate that user's feed, are a ubiquitous and central feature in online social networks. While they are a central piece of our modern digital infrastructure, many modern approaches are opaque black boxes, making them difficult to audit, understand, and assess the trustworthiness of. In this paper we present an exact, graph-based approach for generating explanations for decisions made by recommendation systems. We argue that in the risk-sensitive sociotechnical context of user-facing AI such as recommendation systems, explainability is a key pillar for establishing the trustworthiness of models and validating their effectiveness. We propose a technique built on LightGCN like architectures, an influential and popular class of recommendation models. We describe our approach and argue that it provides an appropriate assurance mechanism for these AI systems leading to specific advantages, including interpretable explanations and a theoretically guaranteed measure of explanation fidelity. We conclude by discussing limitations and directions for future research.

title: llm-gemini 0.35
summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist!

title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
summary:
Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available on Google Cloud. 

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

Four ways Argon changes how your business works

1. Hand off your hardest work

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs. 

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” – Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.

2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business

In finance, legal, tax, and other regulated work, calculations and data extraction need to be precise, repeatable, and verifiable. 

For financial quantitative work, Argon can help automate multi-step ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, and variance analyses. It delivers high calculation integrity, citation fidelity, and formula accuracy across quantitative models. The proof is in the numbers: Argon leads on the Vals Index, which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

In legal research, Argon can help legal teams review case law and regulatory filings to pull out verified citations and key precedents. It leads on domain-specific evaluations like Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for legal research and drafting, with strong citation fidelity and direct answers when helping teams evaluate complex legal precedents. 

"Gemini 4 Argon shows how much progress Google has made on agentic legal reasoning. We saw substantial improvements over Gemini 3.1 Pro across our legal agent evaluations, particularly in corporate M&A, data privacy and cybersecurity, and EC/VC. Accuracy also held up on long-document analysis, an encouraging result for lawyers working through detailed transactional matters." – Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research, Harvey.

“We collaborated with Google on NowAI-Bench to help shape Gemini 4 for key enterprise work. In early access, it delivered roughly 20% improved task success than Gemini 3.8 Flash, with standout gains in HR and customer service. On the ServiceNow AI Platform, our L1 Service Desk AI specialist brings Google’s most advanced intelligence, governed and secure, turning tasks into fully autonomous work.” - Nenshad Bardoliwalla, Senior Vice President, AI Products, ServiceNow.

3. Build and ship products faster

Argon is built to handle complex, multi-step projects from start to finish. Our customers consistently ask for intelligence that can break down goals, track progress, and update multiple files at the same time.

"Gemini 4 Argon handles complex tasks reliably, from 3D games to rich animations. In Figma Make, it helps teams turn their most ambitious, multi-step ideas into impressive prototypes.” – Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer, Figma. 

To see how well Argon handles this, we put it to work on our own tools. The team behind our open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) set out to reduce framework overhead and improve code performance while maintaining full compatibility with existing applications. Working autonomously overnight within automated testing guardrails, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21%. To learn more, read the engineering deep dive here.

Across Google, engineering teams using Argon in Google Antigravity have increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% while cutting code rollbacks by nearly a third. The Chrome team used Argon to finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files in Chromium's 40 million-line codebase, completing months of work in weeks. Argon's improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision and visual coding also make it faster to go from idea to working prototype. 

For more advanced algorithms, our code optimization and discovery agent AlphaEvolve uses Argon to deliver strong performance improvements across real-world enterprise workloads, including factory scheduling, logistics, game code speed-ups, and chip layout — as well as complex mathematical benchmarks, and more. 

To learn how to best use Argon, check out the developer's guide.

4. Stronger defense for your code and business 

While Argon has cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks such as pentesting and exploitation, you can still take full advantage of Argon’s defensive capabilities using CodeMender to find and fix vulnerabilities, or use Argon with your own security harness. It ties for first place on CWE-Bench v1 with a top score of 68% for remediating security vulnerabilities.

"We are integrating Gemini 4 Argon into MarketingX for automated codebase security audits. In our evaluations, the model successfully identified 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities with 0% fabricated vulnerabilities across verified claims. This precision unlocks proactive, code-level security for our customers before deployment.” - Yunus Emre, Chief AI Officer of AI Lab, HubX.

Security also means being able to trust Argon inside your own environment. Argon is our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior. It leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%. That matters when Argon reads email, documents and webpages that may contain hidden malicious instructions. 

We are also releasing Argon without cyber guardrails to a select set of trusted defenders, which allows for testing a full breadth of cybersecurity capabilities. Trusted defenders are vetted through our Fairwind Program, a limited access initiative that provides government, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners exclusive, unmitigated access to advanced  models. 

Enterprise customers and partners in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

Leaders from Amplitude, Deloitte, and Rakuten share Gemini 4 Argon results

Get started

Starting today, Gemini 4 Argon is available in Gemini for business on the web, desktop, and mobile. Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in Gemini platform under model ID gemini-4-argon, in Google AI Studio, and in Google Antigravity.

Argon launches at an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off. After November 30, standard pricing of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens will apply. Review the model card and developer guide for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

Cyber defenders can join us at Security Summit to learn how to use Gemini 4 Argon to defend against machine-speed threats and automate remediation.

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
summary:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

Explicit lazy imports

I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

Unpacking in comprehensions

The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:

lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}

PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.

A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):

sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

uv self update

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

uv python install 3.15

And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

uv python pin --global 3.15

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

uv run python --version

I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15

Then I can confirm the version like this:

datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq

Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.

datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

  • setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.

I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
summary:
Deno is joining Cloudflare

The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.

Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)

The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.

Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:

It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.

I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.

My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.

Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off.

Via Hacker News

  • Added autoCompactWindow to subagent frontmatter and --agents definitions, so a subagent can auto-compact earlier than the main conversation's window
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_SUBAGENT_MODEL to run every workflow agent on one model while other subagents keep theirs
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS environment variable to set a longer maximum delay for the backoff when retrying an overloaded (529) request
  • Added a note in /plugin on a plugin whose hooks are left out because another enabled plugin has the same name
  • Added an allow_large option to the Read tool so Claude can read a text file past the usual size limits in one call when it needs the whole file and the context has room
  • Fixed managed-settings PreToolUse hooks that deny a tool call with "continue": false, and managed prompt hooks that block one, refusing the call but not ending the turn
  • Fixed PostToolUse hooks in managed settings not applying updatedMCPToolOutput in some sessions
  • Fixed headless sessions starting a folder's .mcp.json or plugin MCP server that was switched off for that folder, after changing directory or reloading plugins
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway that serves allowedProviders with "gateway" locking out laptops that name that gateway in user settings
  • Fixed a saved Claude apps gateway sign-in being ignored on machines whose managed settings set forceLoginMethod to gateway with no forceLoginGatewayUrl (regression in 2.1.295)
  • Fixed --teleport opening an empty conversation when the session's history could not be read
  • Fixed token counts for Haiku 5.5 and other models that take only adaptive thinking, which failed behind some gateways and were counted with budget thinking elsewhere
  • Fixed resumed subagents being told that the user rejected a tool call that a session shutdown had interrupted
  • Fixed hook output being altered when it contained text resembling a plugin hint tag
  • Fixed secret redaction in shared transcripts and debug logs missing some values that follow a key with no value, including in JSON written inside a shell string
  • Fixed a stray 52;c;… escape sequence printed on screen after copying in older VTE-based terminals such as MATE Terminal
  • Fixed toasts and notifications waiting unseen for as long as the /diff panel or dialog was open
  • Fixed Esc or an interrupt during a UserPromptSubmit hook or a mod's prompt.submit hook ending headless sessions, clearing the typed prompt, or letting the unchecked prompt through
  • Fixed SessionStart hooks of a plugin loaded after a headless session starts being skipped when a different plugin with the same name, or another spelling of it, had already run
  • Fixed claude self-hosted-runner printing misleading errors when registration is refused: it now names the org admin setting, or says a restarted on-demand runner needs a fresh work order
  • Fixed a self-hosted runner session's git fetch, pull and push failing while another session of the same repository starts on a runner with --capacity above 1
  • Fixed workflow scripts silently truncating results, agent options and other values nested deeper than about 20,000 levels, and deeply nested results writing huge task output files
  • Fixed a plugin's served $ methods running in the main session's working directory instead of the calling agent's, and ignoring the turn their calling hook holds
  • Fixed $.agent.register succeeding from a mod's hook that was still running after the mod was reloaded or removed; the call is now refused
  • Fixed $.http.fetch in mods refusing a HEAD request when the response declares a Content-Length over the 4 MiB body limit
  • Fixed claude plugin marketplace add, marketplace update and plugin install failing with an internal error for a marketplace named like constructor; add now refuses such names clearly
  • Fixed a plugin secret named constructor or prototype being deleted by the next save of that plugin's options
  • Fixed cloud sessions skipping auto mode's checks on Claude in Chrome actions that a saved permission allows when their feature flags had not loaded
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a finished turn after a restart when an MCP tool result had ended that turn
  • Fixed Bash permission checks auto-approving some commands that assign the BASH_ARGV0 shell variable and then use it; these now prompt for approval
  • Fixed Edit and NotebookEdit replacing every non-ASCII character in files that are not valid UTF-8 (Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GBK); such edits are now refused
  • Fixed a prompt sent just after ← being run twice, once unseen in the foreground, when the background service was slow to answer
  • Fixed a prompt sent while SessionStart hooks were still running vanishing when ← moved the session to the background; it is still not sent, but ↑ now brings it back
  • Fixed a late-loading plugin's SessionStart hook output reaching the new conversation after /clear in headless sessions
  • Fixed PowerShell commands not seeing variables that hooks write to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE (when the file holds only plain assignments)
  • Fixed Claude calling cloud sessions non-interactive and suggesting /mcp or claude mcp when an MCP server needs authentication
  • Fixed /code-review ending on a raw JSON array in cloud sessions, the Agent SDK and IDE integrations; the findings now print as a numbered list
  • Fixed auto mode occasionally refusing one update to your own artifact, saying its sharing had changed when it had not
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai never finishing their install, and being downloaded again at every sync, when several sessions share a config directory
  • Fixed a plugin synced from claude.ai being disabled when the marketplace dependency it declares was also synced from claude.ai
  • Fixed a startup hang on macOS when plugin paths copied from a Linux machine pointed under /home
  • Fixed the Workflow tool refusing script files with CRLF line endings, such as files checked out on Windows
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry tool_result events missing git_commit_id after git commit -q or git -C <dir> commit
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping a message from the saved transcript when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029)
  • Fixed claude purge leaving a prompt in the history file when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029)
  • Windows: Fixed PowerShell commands longer than about 1 KB always asking for permission, so allow rules and read-only detection now apply up to 32 KB
  • Windows: Fixed stdio MCP servers being force-killed at shutdown; stdin now closes first and the process tree is killed only if the server is still running after 300 ms
  • Windows: Fixed claude plugin install failing for GitHub owner/repo plugin sources on machines with no GitHub SSH key; the clone is now retried over HTTPS
  • Windows: Fixed rm -rf /c/Users/<name> in Git Bash not asking in bypass permissions mode
  • Improved fullscreen mode: the link under the mouse pointer is now underlined to show it can be opened
  • Improved transcript toggle (ctrl+o) responsiveness in code-heavy conversations by caching syntax-highlighted code blocks
  • Improved Claude Desktop's Code tab behind a Claude apps gateway: when a session can't start, including on a machine not set up for the gateway's code settings, the reason shows as a reply
  • Improved the errors for a refused cloud session: they now say why your organization's policy couldn't be loaded, and name an API key or auth token that overrides your claude.ai login
  • Improved --debug output to name unrecognized frontmatter fields in custom agent files, with a hint for likely typos
  • Improved auto mode: a tool call that wasn't run because auto mode's check had no usable answer now shows as a dim "Not run" row instead of a red error
  • Improved --debug output for hooks: command hooks on tool calls, prompts, SessionStart and Stop now log their command, plugin, outcome and duration when they finish, so a slow hook is identifiable
  • Improved CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC: a large transcript file is no longer rewritten when that would free under 10% of it
  • Updated /cost, the status line, --max-budget-usd and the SDK's cost figures to price Sonnet 5.5 cache reads at $0.10 per million tokens (was $0.20)
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill: lighter violet for the seventh series in light mode, softer primary text in dark mode, and compact y-axis labels like 1K
  • Changed the default limit on MCP tool descriptions sent up front and on MCP server instructions from 2,048 to 4,096 characters
  • Changed ←: a turn or ! command started while the session moves to the background is now stopped instead of finishing out of sight
  • [VSCode] Fixed claudeCode.spinnerVerbs missing from the extension's settings, so settings.json now completes and validates it; a malformed value no longer breaks the chat panel
  • [VSCode] Changed Claude in Chrome to ask before browser actions in every session, including one connected with @browser, as the terminal does; allowing a site for the session stops repeat asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed chat links written as a full Windows path, such as C:\repo\file.ts or file:///C:/repo/file.ts, not opening the file on Windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the working indicator still animating when reduced motion is turned on in your OS, in VS Code, or with the prefersReducedMotion setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt cache clock reading warm after the panel caught up on messages late, such as after the display was off or a remote window reconnected
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a status filter to the Sessions and Runners lists on a self-hosted environment's Activity tab in admin settings; you can pick several statuses at once
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed every cloud session waiting for a self-hosted runner showing the same queue position; each now shows how many sessions are ahead of it
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a message you send while Claude is still replying in a cloud session jumping above that reply when it finishes; it now stays below it, including after a reload
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude in Slack to show the footer with the session link, model and cost only on its newest reply in a thread; the reply before it drops the footer
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed links to URLs that contain parentheses breaking in some of Claude's Slack replies and task checklists, which showed stray bracket text and opened the wrong page
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude's Slack replies drawing color swatches beside codes that only look like hex colors, such as six-digit pull request numbers
  • [Claude Tag] Added creating, editing and deleting workspace and channel memory files on the Activity page's Memory tab for members with the Claude Tag Admin permission
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the plugin confirmation card Claude posts in a Slack channel showing a plugin's ID instead of its name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack posting a card to remove a plugin the channel's own settings don't include; it now explains where the plugin comes from instead
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes losing its reply when a session in a self-hosted environment moved to a new runner partway through a task
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review check sometimes staying "in progress" on a pull request after the review finished; it now shows the review's result
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review admin settings to say why a setting couldn't be saved, such as a policy restriction, instead of a generic failure message
